title: Food Preparation Basics
subtitle: Every cut is a decision about time.
objectives: Explain why cut size changes cooking time
Measure dry and liquid ingredients correctly

cards.title: Every cut is a decision about time
cards.text: Shape is not decoration. A thin piece cooks faster, so the cut decides what finishes together.

cards.title: Even size beats small size
cards.text: The goal is not fine. It is equal.
points: **Equal pieces finish together.**
**Uneven pieces give you burnt and raw** in the same spoonful.
**Smaller means faster**, in every method.
**More surface means more browning.**

cards.title: Five cuts and one grip
cards.text: Tap each one. The last button is the grip that protects your fingers.

question.text: Why does even sizing matter more than fine chopping?
question.explain: Uneven gives you burnt and raw at once.

cards.title: Dry and liquid are measured differently
cards.text: The same cup gives two different answers if you use it wrong.
points: **Dry:** fill past the top, then level it off with a straight edge.
**Do not pack flour.** Do pack brown sugar. Recipes assume it.
**Liquid:** a clear jug, read at eye level.
**Looking down at a jug** reads high every time.

question.text: How do you measure a cup of flour?
options: Fill past the top and level it off
question.explain: Packing flour can add a third more than the recipe wanted.

cards.title: Wash, then cut. In that order
cards.text: The order matters more than it sounds.
points: **Wash under running water**, not in a standing bowl.
**Cutting first drags surface dirt** into the middle.
**Scrub root vegetables**; do not soak them.
**Dry leaves before cutting** or they bruise.

cards.title: Surface area is why brake discs are vented
cards.text: The same fact that makes thin vegetables cook fast cools a brake.
points: **More surface, faster heat exchange.**
**Vented discs expose more metal to air.**
**Julienne exposes more vegetable to heat.**
**One rule, two machines.**

cards.title: Sharpening is a geometry job
cards.text: A blade is two surfaces meeting at an angle, and sharpening is rebuilding that angle.
points: **A dull edge is a rounded edge**, not a worn one.
**A whetstone grinds the angle back.**
**A honing rod straightens** a bent edge, not a blunt one.
**Two different tools.** Two different problems.

question.text: Why does even sizing matter more than fine chopping?
question.explain: Uneven pieces give you burnt and raw in the same spoonful.

cards.title: One carrot, five decisions
cards.alt: Five piles on a board: carrot slices, cubes, matchsticks, minced garlic and fine green leaf ribbons
cards.text: Slice, dice, julienne, mince, chiffonade. Each pile cooks in a different length of time.

cards.title: Repeat it until it is boring
cards.text: Knife skill is one motion, done enough times.
points: **The rock-and-slide of a chef's knife** is a single motion.
**Slow and even first.** Speed comes last.
**Exactly how a jab is learned.**
**Nobody got fast by starting fast.**

cards.title: What to remember
points: Equal pieces matter more than fine pieces.
Slice, dice, julienne, mince, chiffonade. Each is a time decision.
Level dry measures off; read liquids at eye level.
Wash before cutting; use the claw grip.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 5 TLE. The cuts are taught as time decisions rather than as vocabulary, and the week's key correction is that equal matters more than fine. Uneven pieces give burnt and raw in the same spoonful, which is the actual failure he will meet. Measuring gets its own card because the flour error (packing it) silently adds up to a third more than the recipe wanted, and because the eye-level rule for liquids is a one-second habit. The car lens links surface area to vented brake discs, which is the same physics as a julienne and is the kind of cross-subject link that makes a home-economics fact stick.
discussion: Ask why equal size beats small size.
Ask him to measure a cup of flour and explain each step.
Ask what the difference is between honing and sharpening.
Ask why washing comes before cutting.
extension: Have him cut one carrot five ways and time each in boiling water.
Have him weigh a packed cup of flour against a levelled one.
misconceptions: "Finer is always better." Equal is what matters.
"Pack the cup for an accurate measure." Not for flour.
"A honing rod sharpens a knife." It straightens a bent edge.
